intro: Hi! You already know put it off and look after her. Now you'll learn new phrasal verbs for work and study (bring it up, deal with it), three-word ones like come up with and put up with, and eight everyday idioms like break the ice. Warm-up: what's something annoying you have to put up with every day?
teachingNotes: Build on b1-phrasal-verbs: the learner knows 17 B1 verbs (set up, carry on, put off, call off, look into, fill in, hand in, get on with, look after, look forward to, run into, turn down, break down, run out of, give up, sort out, find out) and the two lists 'put it off' (splits) vs 'look after her' (never splits). Recap that in one line; don't re-teach those verbs. Use A0–B1 grammar only (no third conditional, wish, causative, past modals, participle clauses, non-defining relatives). Don't teach the phrasal-verb vs Latin-verb register choice (find out → discover): that's b2-formal-informal-vocab.

Separable (new): bring up a topic (mengangkat; also membesarkan anak), point out (menunjukkan, menyampaikan), work out (menemukan jawaban / cara; without object = olahraga), take over (mengambil alih; take over from = menggantikan), turn up the volume (membesarkan). Pronouns it / them / me / him / her MUST go in the middle; a noun may go either side; a long object or a that- / how- clause tends to go after the small word (tendency, don't test). Common error: *'Can you pick up me at seven?' → pick me up (Indonesian 'jemput saya' puts the person right after the verb).

Inseparable (new): deal with (menangani; *'deal it with', *'deal it'), go through (memeriksa / membahas satu per satu; also mengalami), stand for (singkatan dari), see to (mengurus; a little formal / British). turn up = arrive has no object (American often 'show up'); contrast with turn the music up. Teach the dictionary trick (pick sb/sth up vs deal with sth) and the tendency (with / for / after / into / through usually don't split) as a tendency, not a rule.

Three-part verbs never split (all those in this lesson): come up with, put up with, get away with, catch up with, keep up with, cut down on (+ B1 look forward to, run out of, get on with). Common errors: *'She came up a great idea' → came up with; *'I look forward to meet you' → to meeting (to is part of the phrase; Indonesian 'untuk'); *'put it up with'. Dropping a word changes the meaning (come up = muncul, put up = memasang). keep up with (stay level) vs catch up with (reach after being behind): only test clear contexts.

Idioms: break the ice (mencairkan suasana: same image in Indonesian), a piece of cake (gampang banget), under the weather (kurang enak badan: not about weather), on the same page (sepaham, 'satu frekuensi'), cost an arm and a leg (mahal banget, selangit), hit the nail on the head (tepat sekali), call it a day (sudahan dulu), the ball is in your court (sekarang giliranmu). Words are fixed (*'a piece of cakes'); only tense / person / possessive change. Idioms are informal: fine in conversation and chats, some in meetings, but avoid them in formal writing (cover letters, reports, essays) and don't overuse them.

Test meaning from context with clearly different distractors (illness vs rain vs workload), and form with one clear answer. Don't add more idioms or phrasal verbs unless the learner asks; if they do, give the meaning briefly and say whether it splits.

keyPoints.title: Split or never split
keyPoints.explanation: Some phrasal verbs split: a noun can go after the small word or in the middle, but it / them / me / him / her must go in the middle: bring it up, point them out, work it out, take it over, turn it up, pick me up (not 'pick up me'). Others never split: the object always goes at the end: deal with it, go through it, stand for, see to it. turn up (= arrive) has no object. A good dictionary shows it: pick sb/sth up splits, deal with sth doesn't.

examples.en: Can I bring up the salary issue at today's meeting?
examples.id: Boleh saya angkat soal gaji di rapat hari ini?

examples.en: The project? Sari is going to take it over next month.
examples.id: Proyeknya? Sari yang akan mengambil alih bulan depan.

examples.en: The difficult client? Don't worry, Pak Hasan will deal with him.
examples.id: Klien yang sulit itu? Tenang, Pak Hasan yang akan menanganinya.

id.title: Bisa dipisah atau tidak
id.explanation: Sebagian phrasal verb bisa dipisah: kata benda boleh di belakang kata kecil atau di tengah, tapi it / them / me / him / her harus di tengah: bring it up, point them out, work it out, take it over, turn it up, pick me up (bukan 'pick up me'). Yang lain tidak pernah dipisah: objeknya selalu di akhir: deal with it, go through it, stand for, see to it. turn up (= datang) tidak punya objek. Kamus yang bagus menunjukkannya: pick sb/sth up bisa dipisah, deal with sth tidak.

keyPoints.title: Three-word phrasal verbs
keyPoints.explanation: come up with (menemukan ide), put up with (tahan dengan), get away with (lolos), catch up with (menyusul), keep up with (tidak ketinggalan), cut down on (mengurangi), plus look forward to, run out of and get on with from B1. They never split: put up with it. After the last word comes a noun, it / him, or -ing: look forward to meeting you (not 'to meet'). Don't drop a word: came up with an idea (not 'came up an idea').

examples.en: Bu Ani came up with a great idea for the company's anniversary.
examples.id: Bu Ani menemukan ide bagus untuk ulang tahun perusahaan.

examples.en: How do you put up with the traffic in Jakarta every day?
examples.id: Gimana kamu bisa tahan dengan macetnya Jakarta setiap hari?

examples.en: I'm trying to cut down on fried food.

id.title: Phrasal verb tiga kata
id.explanation: come up with (menemukan ide), put up with (tahan dengan), get away with (lolos), catch up with (menyusul), keep up with (tidak ketinggalan), cut down on (mengurangi), ditambah look forward to, run out of dan get on with dari B1. Semuanya tidak pernah dipisah: put up with it. Setelah kata terakhirnya datang kata benda, it / him, atau -ing: look forward to meeting you (bukan 'to meet'). Jangan buang satu kata pun: came up with an idea (bukan 'came up an idea').

keyPoints.title: Common idioms
keyPoints.explanation: An idiom is a fixed group of words with a meaning you can't guess from each word: break the ice (mencairkan suasana), a piece of cake (gampang banget), under the weather (kurang enak badan), on the same page (sepaham), cost an arm and a leg (mahal banget), hit the nail on the head (tepat sekali), call it a day (sudahan dulu), the ball is in your court (sekarang giliranmu). Don't change the words, only the verb's tense. Use them in conversation, not in formal writing, and don't overuse them.

examples.en: On the first day of the training, the trainer played a quiz game to break the ice.
examples.id: Di hari pertama pelatihan, trainernya mengadakan permainan kuis untuk mencairkan suasana.

examples.en: A wedding in a five-star hotel costs an arm and a leg.
examples.id: Pesta pernikahan di hotel bintang lima harganya selangit.

examples.en: We've sent them our best price. Now the ball is in their court.
examples.id: Kami sudah kirim harga terbaik. Sekarang giliran mereka yang memutuskan.

id.title: Idiom umum
id.explanation: Idiom adalah kelompok kata tetap yang artinya tidak bisa ditebak dari tiap katanya: break the ice (mencairkan suasana), a piece of cake (gampang banget), under the weather (kurang enak badan), on the same page (sepaham), cost an arm and a leg (mahal banget), hit the nail on the head (tepat sekali), call it a day (sudahan dulu), the ball is in your court (sekarang giliranmu). Jangan ubah kata-katanya, hanya tense kata kerjanya. Pakai dalam percakapan, bukan di tulisan formal, dan jangan berlebihan.

independentPractice.hint: For example: I want to cut down on coffee because I can't sleep at night.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: The salary issue is important, so please bring up it at the next team meeting.
acceptableAnswers: the salary issue is important so please bring it up at the next team meeting
please bring it up at the next team meeting
bring it up at the next team meeting
bring it up
the salary issue is important so please bring the issue up at the next team meeting
the salary issue is important so please bring up the issue at the next team meeting
assessment.rubric: Correct: ... please bring it up at the next team meeting (bring up splits, so it goes in the middle). Repeating a noun ('bring up the issue' / 'bring the issue up') = 100. 'bring up it' unchanged = 0. 'bring it' (up dropped) = 20. 'bring it on' or another small word = 0.

assessment.prompt: Put the words through, it and go in the right order: The contract is twenty pages long. Before you sign it, please ___ carefully.
acceptableAnswers: go through it
assessment.rubric: Correct: go through it (go through never splits, so it goes at the end). 'go it through' = 0 (this is the mistake being tested). Any other order = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with a three-word phrasal verb in the past simple (it means menemukan / memunculkan ide): We needed a name for our new food delivery app, and Dimas ___ a brilliant one in five minutes.
acceptableAnswers: came up with
dimas came up with a brilliant one
assessment.rubric: Correct: came up with. 'come up with' = 60 (the past is needed: came). 'came up' (with dropped) = 20 (came up = muncul, a different meaning). 'thought of' = 50 (correct English, but the task asks for a three-word phrasal verb). 'comed up with' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake in this email and write the corrected sentence: 'Dear Bu Ani, Thank you for the interview yesterday. I look forward to hear from you. Kind regards, Sari'
acceptableAnswers: i look forward to hearing from you
look forward to hearing from you
i am looking forward to hearing from you
i'm looking forward to hearing from you
im looking forward to hearing from you
assessment.rubric: Correct: I look forward to hearing from you (to is part of look forward to, so -ing follows). 'I'm looking forward to hearing from you' = 100 (a little less formal, still fine). 'look forward to heard' = 0. 'look forward hearing' = 40 (to dropped). Sentence unchanged = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete with a three-word phrasal verb that means mengurangi: My doctor says I drink too much coffee, so from now on I'm going to ___ it: just one cup a day.
acceptableAnswers: cut down on
cut back on
assessment.rubric: Correct: cut down on ('cut back on' is also correct). 'cut down' (on dropped) = 50. 'cut it down on' = 30 (three-word verbs never split). 'give up' = 0 (that means stop completely, but she'll still drink one cup). 'reduce' = 40 (correct meaning, but not a phrasal verb).

assessment.prompt: Read the chat: 'Rina: How was the TOEFL test this morning? Budi: Honestly? It was a piece of cake.' Did Budi find the test difficult? Write yes or no.
acceptableAnswers: no
no he didn't
no he did not
no he didnt
assessment.rubric: Correct: no. a piece of cake = gampang banget, so the test was very easy for Budi. 'yes' = 0. An answer about cake or food = 0.

assessment.prompt: Complete the idiom with one word: It's five o'clock and the important tasks are done. Let's call it a ___ and finish the rest tomorrow.
acceptableAnswers: day
assessment.rubric: Correct: day (call it a day = sudahan dulu, stop working for today). 'night' = 50 (call it a night exists, but it's for the evening; at five o'clock after work it's call it a day). Any other word = 0.

material.title: Verbs that split: bring it up, point it out

blocks.text:
**Quick recap** from B1: some phrasal verbs **split** (*put it off, hand it in*: it goes in the middle), others **never split** (*look after her, run out of it*: the word goes at the end).

Here are five new ones that **split**. They're very common at work and on campus:
- **bring up** a topic = mengangkat, menyinggung (a topic in a meeting or a conversation). It also means membesarkan (children): *I was brought up in Medan.*
- **point out** = menunjukkan, menyampaikan (a mistake, a problem, a fact)
- **work out** = menemukan (jawaban / cara), memecahkan (a problem, a price, how to do something). Without an object it means olahraga: *I work out at the gym.*
- **take over** = mengambil alih (a company, a project, a job). *take over from* someone = menggantikan seseorang.
- **turn up** the volume / the music = membesarkan (suara) (the opposite of *turn down*)

The rule is the one you know from *turn it off*: a **noun** (a word for a thing or person, like *the issue, the report*) can go **after** the small word **or in the middle**, but **it, them, me, him, her, us** (short words that replace a noun) **must go in the middle**.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat** dari B1: ada phrasal verb yang **bisa dipisah** (*put it off, hand it in*: it di tengah), ada yang **tidak pernah dipisah** (*look after her, run out of it*: katanya di akhir).

Ini lima yang baru dan **bisa dipisah**. Semuanya sangat umum di kantor dan di kampus:
- **bring up** sebuah topik = mengangkat, menyinggung (topik di rapat atau obrolan). Bisa juga berarti membesarkan (anak): *I was brought up in Medan.*
- **point out** = menunjukkan, menyampaikan (kesalahan, masalah, fakta)
- **work out** = menemukan (jawaban / cara), memecahkan (masalah, harga, cara melakukan sesuatu). Tanpa objek artinya olahraga: *I work out at the gym.*
- **take over** = mengambil alih (perusahaan, proyek, pekerjaan). *take over from* seseorang = menggantikan seseorang.
- **turn up** volume / musik = membesarkan (suara) (kebalikan dari *turn down*)

Aturannya sama seperti *turn it off* yang sudah kamu kenal: **kata benda** (kata untuk benda atau orang, seperti *the issue, the report*) boleh **di belakang** kata kecil **atau di tengah**, tapi **it, them, me, him, her, us** (kata pendek pengganti kata benda) **harus di tengah**.

rows.id: Boleh saya angkat soal gaji di rapat hari ini?

rows.id: Rina menunjukkan dua kesalahan di anggarannya.

blocks.text: Indonesian trap: in Indonesian the person always comes right after the verb (*jemput **saya***), so many learners say 'Can you pick up me at seven?' ✗. With a verb that splits, **me / him / her / it** go **in the middle**: **Can you pick me up at seven?** ✓. The same with the new verbs: *bring **it** up, point **them** out, work **it** out, take **it** over*.

id.text: Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: dalam bahasa Indonesia orangnya selalu langsung setelah kata kerja (*jemput **saya***), jadi banyak yang bilang 'Can you pick up me at seven?' ✗. Dengan kata kerja yang bisa dipisah, **me / him / her / it** ditaruh **di tengah**: **Can you pick me up at seven?** ✓. Sama dengan kata kerja yang baru: *bring **it** up, point **them** out, work **it** out, take **it** over*.

blocks.text: Two tendencies (not strict rules): with a **long** object, natives usually put it **after** the small word: *She pointed out **three problems with the new schedule***. And with a whole clause (*that …, how …, what …*), the small word stays next to the verb: *He pointed out **that the deadline was Friday***. Only the short words (it, them, me …) **must** go in the middle.

id.text: Dua kecenderungan (bukan aturan ketat): kalau objeknya **panjang**, penutur asli biasanya menaruhnya **di belakang** kata kecil: *She pointed out **three problems with the new schedule***. Dan kalau yang mengikuti adalah anak kalimat (*that …, how …, what …*), kata kecilnya tetap menempel pada kata kerja: *He pointed out **that the deadline was Friday***. Hanya kata pendek (it, them, me …) yang **wajib** di tengah.

blocks.prompt: Rina found two mistakes in the slides. Which sentence is correct?
options: She pointed out them before the client meeting.
She pointed them out before the client meeting.
She pointed them before the client meeting out.
blocks.explain: point out splits, and them must go in the middle: pointed them out. 'pointed out them' is the 'pick up me' mistake, and out can't move to the end of the sentence.

id.prompt: Rina menemukan dua kesalahan di slide. Kalimat mana yang benar?
id.explain: point out bisa dipisah, dan them harus di tengah: pointed them out. 'pointed out them' adalah kesalahan yang sama dengan 'pick up me', dan out tidak boleh pindah ke akhir kalimat.

id.title: Kata kerja yang bisa dipisah: bring it up, point it out

material.title: Verbs that never split: deal with it, go through it

blocks.text:
These phrasal verbs **never split**: the person or thing always goes **at the end**, even *it, them, him, her*:
- **deal with** = menangani, mengurus (a problem, complaints, a difficult customer): *deal with **it***
- **go through** = memeriksa / membahas satu per satu (a contract, a report, a list). It also means mengalami (a hard time): *She went through a difficult year.*
- **stand for** = singkatan dari: *What does KRL stand for?* — *Kereta Rel Listrik.*
- **see to** = mengurus (a small job, so you don't have to): *I'll see to **it**.* (a little formal, more British)

And some have **no object at all**, so there's nothing to move: **turn up** = datang, muncul (often late or by surprise): *Budi turned up an hour late.* (Not the same as *turn the music up*!) American English often says **show up**.

id.text:
Phrasal verb berikut **tidak pernah dipisah**: orang atau bendanya selalu **di akhir**, termasuk *it, them, him, her*:
- **deal with** = menangani, mengurus (masalah, keluhan, pelanggan yang sulit): *deal with **it***
- **go through** = memeriksa / membahas satu per satu (kontrak, laporan, daftar). Bisa juga berarti mengalami (masa sulit): *She went through a difficult year.*
- **stand for** = singkatan dari: *What does KRL stand for?* — *Kereta Rel Listrik.*
- **see to** = mengurus (pekerjaan kecil, supaya kamu tidak perlu repot): *I'll see to **it**.* (agak formal, lebih British)

Ada juga yang **tidak punya objek sama sekali**, jadi tidak ada yang perlu dipindah: **turn up** = datang, muncul (sering terlambat atau tiba-tiba): *Budi turned up an hour late.* (Beda dengan *turn the music up*!) Bahasa Inggris Amerika sering bilang **show up**.

blocks.text: How can you tell if a phrasal verb splits? **Look in a good dictionary** (Cambridge, Oxford). It shows where the object goes: *pick **sb/sth** up* (sb = somebody, sth = something) means it splits; *deal with **sth*** means it doesn't. A tendency: verbs with **with, for, after, into, through** usually don't split, and verbs with **up, out, off, down, over** often do. But it's only a tendency, so check the dictionary.

id.text: Bagaimana tahu sebuah phrasal verb bisa dipisah atau tidak? **Lihat kamus yang bagus** (Cambridge, Oxford). Kamus menunjukkan letak objeknya: *pick **sb/sth** up* (sb = somebody / seseorang, sth = something / sesuatu) berarti bisa dipisah; *deal with **sth*** berarti tidak bisa. Kecenderungannya: kata kerja dengan **with, for, after, into, through** biasanya tidak dipisah, dan yang dengan **up, out, off, down, over** sering bisa dipisah. Tapi ini hanya kecenderungan, jadi tetap cek kamus.

blocks.text: Indonesian trap: *menanganinya* is one word with *-nya* at the end, so learners write 'deal it' ✗ or 'deal it with' ✗. Keep **with** and put the object after it: **deal with it**.

id.text: Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: *menanganinya* adalah satu kata dengan *-nya* di akhir, jadi banyak yang menulis 'deal it' ✗ atau 'deal it with' ✗. Pertahankan **with** dan taruh objeknya sesudahnya: **deal with it**.

blocks.prompt: A customer at the front desk is shouting. Your manager says:
blocks.explain: deal with never splits, so him goes at the end: I'll deal with him. 'deal him with' splits a verb that doesn't split, and 'deal him' drops with.

id.prompt: Ada pelanggan yang berteriak di meja depan. Manajermu berkata:
id.explain: deal with tidak pernah dipisah, jadi him di akhir: I'll deal with him. 'deal him with' memisahkan kata kerja yang tidak bisa dipisah, dan 'deal him' membuang with.

id.title: Kata kerja yang tidak pernah dipisah: deal with it, go through it

material.title: Three-word phrasal verbs: come up with, put up with …

blocks.text:
You already know three of them from B1: **look forward to**, **run out of**, **get on with**. Here are six more:
- **come up with** = menemukan, memunculkan (an idea, a name, a plan, a solution)
- **put up with** = tahan dengan, sabar menghadapi (something annoying: noise, traffic, a rude colleague)
- **get away with** = lolos (without punishment or criticism)
- **catch up with** = menyusul (people who are ahead of you). In British English also: ketemu lagi dan ngobrol (*catch up with an old friend*)
- **keep up with** = mengikuti, tidak ketinggalan (the class, the news, technology)
- **cut down on** = mengurangi (sugar, coffee, screen time, spending)

Two rules:
1. They **never split**: the object goes at the very end: *put up with **it***, never 'put it up with'.
2. The last word (*with, to, on, of*) is followed by a **noun**, a short word like **it / him**, or a verb with **-ing**: *got away with **cheating***, *looking forward to **meeting** you*.

id.text:
Tiga di antaranya sudah kamu kenal dari B1: **look forward to**, **run out of**, **get on with**. Ini enam lagi:
- **come up with** = menemukan, memunculkan (ide, nama, rencana, solusi)
- **put up with** = tahan dengan, sabar menghadapi (sesuatu yang menyebalkan: bising, macet, rekan kerja yang kasar)
- **get away with** = lolos (tanpa hukuman atau teguran)
- **catch up with** = menyusul (orang yang ada di depanmu). Di bahasa Inggris British juga berarti: ketemu lagi dan ngobrol (*catch up with an old friend*)
- **keep up with** = mengikuti, tidak ketinggalan (pelajaran, berita, teknologi)
- **cut down on** = mengurangi (gula, kopi, waktu main HP, pengeluaran)

Dua aturan:
1. **Tidak pernah dipisah**: objeknya di paling akhir: *put up with **it***, jangan pernah 'put it up with'.
2. Kata terakhirnya (*with, to, on, of*) diikuti **kata benda**, kata pendek seperti **it / him**, atau kata kerja dengan **-ing**: *got away with **cheating***, *looking forward to **meeting** you*.

rows.en: Bu Ani came up with a great idea for the company's anniversary.
rows.id: Bu Ani menemukan ide bagus untuk ulang tahun perusahaan.

rows.en: How do you put up with the traffic in Jakarta every day?
rows.id: Gimana kamu bisa tahan dengan macetnya Jakarta setiap hari?

rows.en: He copied his friend's report and got away with it.
rows.id: Dia menyalin laporan temannya dan lolos begitu saja.

rows.en: Go ahead, I'll catch up with you at the MRT station.
rows.id: Duluan saja, nanti saya susul di stasiun MRT.
rows.note: catch up with = reach someone ahead

rows.en: It's hard to keep up with all the new AI tools.
rows.id: Susah mengikuti semua aplikasi AI yang baru.
rows.note: keep up with = not fall behind

rows.en: I'm trying to cut down on fried food.
rows.id: Saya sedang berusaha mengurangi gorengan.

blocks.text: Don't drop a word: each small word is part of the meaning. **She came up with a great idea** ✓, not 'She came up a great idea' ✗ (*come up* alone = muncul). **I can't put up with the noise** ✓, not 'put up the noise' ✗ (*put up* alone = memasang, like a poster). And *look forward to + -ing*: Indonesian *tidak sabar **untuk** bertemu* leads to 'look forward to meet' ✗ → **look forward to meeting** ✓.

id.text: Jangan buang satu kata pun: setiap kata kecil adalah bagian dari artinya. **She came up with a great idea** ✓, bukan 'She came up a great idea' ✗ (*come up* saja = muncul). **I can't put up with the noise** ✓, bukan 'put up the noise' ✗ (*put up* saja = memasang, seperti memasang poster). Dan *look forward to + -ing*: bahasa Indonesia *tidak sabar **untuk** bertemu* membuat orang menulis 'look forward to meet' ✗ → **look forward to meeting** ✓.

blocks.text: **catch up with** or **keep up with**? Both are about not being behind. **keep up with** = you stay at the same level, you don't fall behind (*It's hard to keep up with the news*). **catch up with** = you're already behind, and you reach the others (*I missed a week, so I need to catch up*). Also: a few rare three-word verbs can split, but none of the ones in this lesson do.

id.text: **catch up with** atau **keep up with**? Keduanya tentang tidak tertinggal. **keep up with** = kamu tetap sejajar, tidak sampai tertinggal (*It's hard to keep up with the news*). **catch up with** = kamu sudah tertinggal, lalu menyusul yang lain (*I missed a week, so I need to catch up*). Catatan: ada beberapa phrasal verb tiga kata yang jarang dipakai yang bisa dipisah, tapi tidak ada satu pun di pelajaran ini.

blocks.prompt: Sari's office is next to a construction site. Her friend asks: "How do you ___ all that noise?"
blocks.explain: put up with = tahan dengan, sabar menghadapi something annoying, like noise. come up with is for ideas, and keep up with is for not falling behind.

id.prompt: Kantor Sari ada di sebelah proyek bangunan. Temannya bertanya. Lengkapi: "How do you ___ all that noise?"
id.explain: put up with = tahan dengan, sabar menghadapi sesuatu yang menyebalkan, seperti suara bising. come up with untuk ide, dan keep up with untuk tidak tertinggal.

material.title: Common idioms: break the ice, under the weather …

blocks.text:
An **idiom** is a fixed group of words whose meaning you **can't guess from each word**. If you translate it word by word, you get nonsense: *under the weather* has nothing to do with the weather. Learn each idiom as one piece, like a new word. Eight very common ones:
- **break the ice** = mencairkan suasana (Indonesian uses the same picture of ice!)
- **a piece of cake** = gampang banget, "kecil"
- **under the weather** = kurang enak badan, agak meriang
- **on the same page** = sepaham, punya pemahaman yang sama, "satu frekuensi"
- **cost an arm and a leg** = mahal banget, harganya selangit
- **hit the nail on the head** = tepat sekali, pas banget (say exactly the right thing)
- **call it a day** = sudahan dulu (stop working for today)
- **the ball is in your court** = sekarang giliranmu (to decide or act)

id.text:
**Idiom** adalah kelompok kata yang tetap, dan artinya **tidak bisa ditebak dari tiap katanya**. Kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata, hasilnya aneh: *under the weather* tidak ada hubungannya dengan cuaca. Hafalkan setiap idiom sebagai satu kesatuan, seperti kosakata baru. Delapan yang sangat umum:
- **break the ice** = mencairkan suasana (bahasa Indonesia juga memakai gambaran es!)
- **a piece of cake** = gampang banget, "kecil"
- **under the weather** = kurang enak badan, agak meriang
- **on the same page** = sepaham, punya pemahaman yang sama, "satu frekuensi"
- **cost an arm and a leg** = mahal banget, harganya selangit
- **hit the nail on the head** = tepat sekali, pas banget (mengatakan hal yang benar-benar tepat)
- **call it a day** = sudahan dulu (berhenti kerja untuk hari ini)
- **the ball is in your court** = sekarang giliranmu (untuk memutuskan atau bertindak)

rows.en: On the first day of the training, the trainer played a quiz game to break the ice.
rows.id: Di hari pertama pelatihan, trainernya mengadakan permainan kuis untuk mencairkan suasana.

rows.en: Don't worry about the new booking app. Using it is a piece of cake.
rows.id: Jangan khawatir soal aplikasi pemesanan yang baru. Cara pakainya gampang banget.
rows.note: a piece of cake = very easy

id.note: a piece of cake = gampang banget

rows.en: Bu Ani isn't coming in today. She's a bit under the weather.
rows.id: Bu Ani tidak masuk hari ini. Dia agak kurang enak badan.
rows.note: under the weather = a little ill

id.note: under the weather = kurang enak badan

rows.en: Before we start the design, let's make sure we're all on the same page.
rows.id: Sebelum mulai desain, pastikan kita semua sepaham dulu.
rows.note: on the same page = agree, understand the same

rows.en: A wedding in a five-star hotel costs an arm and a leg.
rows.id: Pesta pernikahan di hotel bintang lima harganya selangit.
rows.note: cost an arm and a leg = very expensive

id.note: cost an arm and a leg = mahal banget

rows.en: We've sent them our best price. Now the ball is in their court.
rows.id: Kami sudah kirim harga terbaik. Sekarang giliran mereka yang memutuskan.
rows.note: the ball is in their court

blocks.text: Don't guess from the picture in the words. *under the weather* is about **health**, not rain. *a piece of cake* is about something **easy**, not food. *cost an arm and a leg* is about **price**, nobody gets hurt. Read the **context** (the situation around the idiom): *She's under the weather, so she's working from home* → she's a little ill.

id.text: Jangan menebak dari gambaran kata-katanya. *under the weather* itu tentang **kesehatan**, bukan hujan. *a piece of cake* tentang sesuatu yang **mudah**, bukan makanan. *cost an arm and a leg* tentang **harga**, tidak ada yang terluka. Baca **konteksnya** (situasi di sekitar idiom itu): *She's under the weather, so she's working from home* → dia agak sakit.

blocks.prompt: Dimas texts his manager: "Morning, Bu. I'm a bit under the weather today, so I'll work from home." Why is Dimas working from home?
options: It's raining heavily in his area.
blocks.explain: under the weather = kurang enak badan: Dimas feels a little ill. The idiom has nothing to do with rain, and nothing in the message is about his workload.

id.prompt: Dimas mengirim pesan ke manajernya: "Morning, Bu. I'm a bit under the weather today, so I'll work from home." Kenapa Dimas bekerja dari rumah?
id.explain: under the weather = kurang enak badan: Dimas agak sakit. Idiom ini tidak ada hubungannya dengan hujan, dan pesannya tidak menyebut soal banyaknya pekerjaan.

id.title: Idiom umum: break the ice, under the weather …

material.title: Using idioms well (and when not to)

blocks.text:
Three things to know before you use an idiom:
1. **The words are fixed.** Don't change them or make them plural: *a piece of cake* (not 'a piece of cakes', not 'a slice of cake'), *cost an arm and a leg* (not 'a hand and a leg').
2. **Only the grammar around it changes**: the verb takes its normal tense and -s (*the game **broke** the ice, it **costs** an arm and a leg, we **called** it a day*), and the possessive changes with the person (*the ball is in **your / their** court*).
3. **Idioms are informal.** They're great in conversation, chats and friendly emails. Some are fine in meetings too (*on the same page, the ball is in your court*). But **avoid them in formal writing**: a job application, a report, an essay or a formal email. There, say it plainly: *The test was very easy. I am unwell today.*

id.text:
Tiga hal yang perlu kamu tahu sebelum memakai idiom:
1. **Kata-katanya tetap.** Jangan diubah atau dijadikan jamak: *a piece of cake* (bukan 'a piece of cakes', bukan 'a slice of cake'), *cost an arm and a leg* (bukan 'a hand and a leg').
2. **Hanya tata bahasa di sekitarnya yang berubah**: kata kerjanya memakai tense dan -s seperti biasa (*the game **broke** the ice, it **costs** an arm and a leg, we **called** it a day*), dan kata kepemilikannya ikut orangnya (*the ball is in **your / their** court*).
3. **Idiom itu informal.** Cocok untuk obrolan, chat dan email santai. Beberapa juga wajar dipakai di rapat (*on the same page, the ball is in your court*). Tapi **hindari di tulisan formal**: surat lamaran kerja, laporan, esai atau email resmi. Di sana, katakan dengan lugas: *The test was very easy. I am unwell today.*

rows.en: Chat: "Thanks, guys! Let's call it a day and get some bakso."
rows.id: Chat: "Makasih, semua! Sudahan dulu yuk, terus makan bakso."

rows.en: Formal email: "I am unable to attend today's meeting because I am unwell."
rows.id: Email resmi: "Saya tidak dapat menghadiri rapat hari ini karena sedang tidak enak badan."

rows.en: Cover letter: "I learn new software quickly."
rows.id: Surat lamaran: "Saya cepat mempelajari perangkat lunak baru."
rows.note: not 'new software is a piece of cake for me'

id.note: bukan 'new software is a piece of cake for me'

blocks.text: **Don't overuse them.** One idiom in a conversation sounds natural; five in a row sounds like a textbook, or like you're joking. It's better to use a few idioms correctly than many in the wrong place. And when you're not sure an idiom fits, the plain words are always safe.

id.text: **Jangan berlebihan.** Satu idiom dalam percakapan terdengar alami; lima berturut-turut terdengar seperti buku pelajaran, atau seperti sedang bercanda. Lebih baik memakai sedikit idiom dengan tepat daripada banyak tapi di tempat yang salah. Dan kalau kamu ragu sebuah idiom cocok, kata-kata biasa selalu aman.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence fits best in a cover letter for a job at a bank?
options: Working with numbers is a piece of cake for me.
I have three years' experience in financial reporting.
I always hit the nail on the head with numbers.
blocks.explain: A cover letter is formal writing, so the plain sentence without an idiom is best. The other two use informal idioms that sound too casual (and a bit boastful) for a job application.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang paling cocok untuk surat lamaran kerja di bank?
id.explain: Surat lamaran adalah tulisan formal, jadi kalimat lugas tanpa idiom yang paling tepat. Dua kalimat lainnya memakai idiom informal yang terlalu santai (dan agak sombong) untuk surat lamaran.

id.title: Memakai idiom dengan tepat (dan kapan jangan)

resources.title: Something to look forward to: three-word phrasal verbs
resources.note: A short article from the Cambridge Dictionary blog on three-word phrasal verbs like look forward to, come up with, get away with and put up with. It also shows a few that aren't in this lesson (face up to, make up for) and one rare exception that splits.

id.note: Artikel singkat dari blog Cambridge Dictionary tentang phrasal verb tiga kata seperti look forward to, come up with, get away with dan put up with. Ada juga beberapa yang tidak ada di pelajaran ini (face up to, make up for) dan satu pengecualian langka yang bisa dipisah.

id.intro: Hai! Kamu sudah kenal put it off dan look after her. Sekarang kamu akan belajar phrasal verb baru untuk kerja dan kuliah (bring it up, deal with it), yang tiga kata seperti come up with dan put up with, dan delapan idiom sehari-hari seperti break the ice. Pemanasan: hal menyebalkan apa yang harus kamu tahan setiap hari?
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana cara tahu sebuah phrasal verb bisa dipisah atau tidak?
Apa bedanya catch up with dan keep up with?
Bolehkah saya memakai idiom seperti 'a piece of cake' saat wawancara kerja atau di email?
Kenapa 'look forward to hearing' dan bukan 'to hear'?

assessment.pvi-1: Perbaiki kesalahannya: The salary issue is important, so please bring up it at the next team meeting.
assessment.pvi-2: Susun kata through, it dan go dengan urutan yang benar: The contract is twenty pages long. Before you sign it, please ___ carefully.
assessment.pvi-3: Lengkapi dengan phrasal verb tiga kata dalam bentuk past simple (artinya menemukan / memunculkan ide): We needed a name for our new food delivery app, and Dimas ___ a brilliant one in five minutes.
assessment.pvi-4: Perbaiki kesalahan di email ini dan tulis kalimat yang sudah benar: 'Dear Bu Ani, Thank you for the interview yesterday. I look forward to hear from you. Kind regards, Sari'
assessment.pvi-5: Lengkapi dengan phrasal verb tiga kata yang artinya mengurangi: My doctor says I drink too much coffee, so from now on I'm going to ___ it: just one cup a day.
assessment.pvi-6: Baca chat-nya: 'Rina: How was the TOEFL test this morning? Budi: Honestly? It was a piece of cake.' Apakah menurut Budi tesnya sulit? Tulis yes atau no.
assessment.pvi-7: Lengkapi idiomnya dengan satu kata bahasa Inggris: It's five o'clock and the important tasks are done. Let's call it a ___ and finish the rest tomorrow.
